Describe a celebration, people and objects with lots of adjectives.
It's 12 May 2033. Today Grete turns 97. Mara and Lena are decorating the common room of the “Am Kollwitzpark” care home. Friedrich is checking the piano.
Lena, where shall we put the long, colourful garland? Above the big door or above the tall window?
Above the window. That way you can see it from the old grand piano.
The old grand piano was tuned yesterday. By a young piano tuner from Pankow. A very nice young man, but he had no idea about Brahms.
Mr Mertens, you look very smart today. Is that a new suit?
A new suit? At ninety-eight you don't buy new suits any more. It's my oldest suit. I wore it in 1960, at the last concert I heard her give. Before the Wall.
And does it still fit you? After seventy-three years?
Almost. Sophie let it out a little. She's a better tailor than she is a doctor, I always say. She doesn't like hearing that.
The fresh flowers have arrived! White lilac, the way Mrs Hoffmann likes it. From Ludwig's little garden.
White lilac. She had a bunch of white lilac in her hands when I first saw her. In 1957. A young pianist, with big eyes and the most beautiful smile in all of Berlin.
Mr Mertens, you're the most romantic man I know. After Grandpa.
After Grandpa? We'll have to settle that. Over a good glass of wine.

The short rule: -e only in the 5 “boxes” N sg. (all genders) and A sg. fem./neuter. Everywhere else: -en.
Where “ein” has no ending (N masc., N/A neuter), the adjective takes over the ending of the definite article:
Traps: “ein alter Flügel” (masc.) versus “ein altes Haus” (neuter). The ending -er / -es “borrows” the letter from der / das.
When there's no article, the adjective shows the case by itself, with the endings of the definite article:
Useful fixed phrases: Herzlichen Glückwunsch! Mit freundlichen Grüßen. Vielen Dank! Guten Appetit! — all with strong declension.
4. Comparative and superlative in front of the noun
The comparative and the superlative get the same endings as any adjective:
Sophie is a better tailor than she is a doctor.
She had the most beautiful smile in all of Berlin.
Irregular forms: gut → besser → der beste; viel → mehr → das meiste; hoch → höher → der höchste (but: der hohe Baum, without the c!).

Wann hat Friedrich Grete zum ersten Mal gesehen?

At three in the afternoon the large common room of the “Am Kollwitzpark” care home was fuller than ever. Above the tall window hung the long, colourful garland, on all the tables there were fresh flowers in little glasses, white lilac from Ludwig's garden, and on the wall hung a big poster painted by Jakob's class: “Happy 97th birthday, dear Mrs Hoffmann!” Underneath, all twenty-six children had signed, some with a little heart, others with a crooked piano key.

Mara had been here since the morning. She had taken the day off, for the first time since she had become ward sister, and her deputy had promised to call her only if the hospital was on fire. Together with Lena she had laid the tables, with white tablecloths that the care home only brought out at Christmas and with the good china, which the manager of the home, Mrs Petersen, had personally taken out of a locked cupboard in the cellar. “For Mrs Hoffmann,” Mrs Petersen had said, “only the best. She's our oldest resident. And the cheekiest.”

Everyone had come. The other residents of the home, in their best clothes, some in wheelchairs, others with walking frames. The carers in their white coats. Ludwig in his dark grey Sunday suit, with the old brass bell in his jacket pocket, just in case. Mara and Jakob, Lena and Andrei, Kuba and Ola, Elif with her parents. Susanne and Peter from Hanover. Mirko from Dresden, with his viola. Sophie from Lübeck, Friedrich's granddaughter, a tall blonde woman with her grandfather's eyes. Even Mrs Becker from the kiosk had come, with an enormous box of chocolates.

Then the door opened and Grete came in. She walked slowly, on Friedrich's arm, in a navy-blue dress with a white pearl necklace she had had since her first big concert. Her white hair was freshly done, her thin cheeks slightly flushed. Since the serious pneumonia in February she had become even more delicate, even smaller, but her eyes were the same as in the old photo from 1956: clear, alert and a little ironic. When she saw so many people, she stopped. “Good heavens,” she said. “Who's died?”

Everyone laughed. Then they sang, all together, out of tune, loudly and from the heart, “Happy Birthday” in German, and Mirko accompanied them on the viola, and the children sang a verse in Romanian that Andrei had taught them, “Mulți ani trăiască” (“Long may she live”), with a pronunciation that brought tears to Andrei's eyes, from laughter and emotion. Grete sat down in the big armchair next to the piano, which had been got ready for her, and listened, with her hands folded.

Sophie sat down next to her grandfather and whispered something in his ear. Friedrich smiled and nodded. Later she told Mara what it had been: “I told him I'd never seen him so happy. In my whole life. When I was a child I thought my grandfather didn't know how to laugh. He was always so serious, so quiet. Now I know he was just waiting.” Mara nodded. She knew that waiting. She had seen it in Grete's eyes, and in Ludwig's, and sometimes, if she was honest, in her own.

There was cake, of course. Andrei had baked an enormous Black Forest gateau, the biggest he had ever made, with ninety-seven little candles, which Elif had lit, all of them, one by one. Grete tried to blow them out, but only managed up to the twelfth. Then the children helped her, all twenty-six at once, and for a moment the room was full of smoke, laughter and applause. Mrs Becker was crying into a big checked handkerchief. Nobody knew exactly why.

Ludwig gave a short speech. He wasn't a good speaker, he knew that, but Grete had insisted. He told how he had got to know her in 1995, when he bought the house and she lived on the fourth floor, a strict old lady who on the very first day had slipped a letter under his door with a list of twelve things that needed repairing in the stairwell. “It took me two years to repair all twelve,” said Ludwig. “And another five years before she invited me for coffee for the first time. But since then she's played the piano for me every Sunday, through the ceiling, whether I wanted it or not.” Everyone laughed, and Grete laughed loudest.

Then it went quiet. Grete stood up, slowly, and Friedrich wanted to help her, but she shook her head. She took the three steps to the piano by herself, sat down on the black stool, adjusted it the way she had done for ninety years and put her hands on the keys. In February she had promised to play the rest of the Brahms sonata on her birthday. Grete Hoffmann had never broken a promise.

She didn't play perfectly. Her fingers were stiff, sometimes they trembled, sometimes a note was missing. But nobody in the room heard the missing notes. They heard a ninety-seven-year-old woman who, as a little girl, had played in the cellar for the other children while the bombs were falling outside. Who had made her debut at twenty at the Konzerthaus. Who had waited sixty-nine years for a man who was now standing next to the piano, in his oldest suit, crying unashamedly. And when she played the last chord, very softly, very delicately, and put her hands in her lap, it was so quiet that you could hear the blackbirds outside in the park.

Nobody clapped. It seemed wrong to clap in that silence. Mirko, the viola player from Dresden, who had played in the biggest concert halls in Europe in his life, sat with his head bowed on his chair, wiping his eyes. Later he told Susanne that he had never heard a Brahms sonata in which every wrong note was right. Susanne understood exactly what he meant. She was thinking of a little girl with pigtails who had read the first whole page of a book slowly and with mistakes, and of a teacher who had written afterwards in red ink: I'm very proud of you.
There. Now I've kept my promise. Friedrich, you shouldn't have cried. It wasn't my best performance. My best was in 1960. You were there.
No, Grete. Today's was the most beautiful. The most beautiful I've ever heard. Because I didn't hear it alone.

Then Elif stood up, little Elif with the gap in her teeth and her serious face, and went to the piano. She was holding a sheet of paper. “Mrs Hoffmann,” she said, “I've written a poem for you. It's not very good. But Mr Lorenz said it's the most honest one he's read this year.” And she read aloud, in her clear child's voice, six short lines about an old lady with white hair who makes music with her hands and about an old gentleman who listens. The last line said: “And when she plays, he becomes young again.”

Grete took the sheet, folded it carefully and put it in the little pocket of her navy-blue dress, right over her heart. “That,” she said, “is the most beautiful birthday present I've received in ninety-seven years. And I've received a great many. And some quite expensive ones.” Then she looked at Elif for a long time, with her clear, ironic gaze. “Do you play an instrument, child?” Elif shook her head. “Then come next Wednesday at four,” said Grete. “We'll start with the piano. I haven't got much time left. We need to hurry.”

Elif looked at her parents, and Mr Yilmaz, the quiet bus driver who never said much, nodded so vigorously that everyone laughed. Mrs Yilmaz whispered something in Turkish, which Elif later translated for everyone: “Mum says she wanted to play the piano too when she was a child, but there was no money for it.” Grete looked at Mrs Yilmaz. “Then you come too,” she said. “Wednesday at four. There's no age limit for mothers. Nor for pianists, for that matter. Look at me.”

In the evening, when all the guests had gone and the carers were clearing the tables, Grete and Friedrich sat alone for a while by the window of the common room. Outside, in Kollwitzpark, the street lamps were coming on, and the white lilac on the tables smelt sweet in the warm evening air. Grete had taken Elif's poem out of her pocket again and was reading it once more, slowly, with her finger under the lines. “Friedrich,” she said without looking up, “I think it was my most beautiful birthday. More beautiful than my twentieth. More beautiful than my fiftieth in Vienna, with the big orchestra.” Friedrich took her hand. “Why?” he asked, even though he knew the answer. Grete folded the poem up again. “Because for the first time I didn't play for an audience,” she said. “But for my family.”
